title: When One Database Isn't Enough
description: Learn why single databases are dangerous, how leader-follower replication works, and what happens when the leader goes down.

segments.text: Let's talk about something that keeps engineers up at night. Your entire application relies on one database. One. If it dies, everything dies. Let me show you why that's terrifying.
Here's your database. Every read, every write, every query — all hitting this one machine. It's a single point of failure. Disk dies? Data gone. Server crashes? Application down.
The solution? Copies. We make copies of the data on multiple machines. If one goes down, the others still have everything. This is replication.

But you can't just have everyone accepting writes — that's chaos. So we pick one database as the leader. It handles all writes. Then we add followers that receive copies of everything the leader writes.
Watch this. A write comes in — 'update user email.' It goes to the leader. The leader writes it, then ships that change to every follower. Now all copies are in sync.
The leader streams its write-ahead log — every change, in order — to the followers. They replay these changes and stay up to date. Reads can go to any follower, spreading the load beautifully.
Now THIS is where it gets interesting. What if a follower is slow? The leader wrote the update, but the follower hasn't received it yet.
segments.thought_prompt: If you read from a lagging follower right after writing to the leader, what would you see?

segments.text: You'd see stale data! You just updated your email, but when you reload the page, the old email shows up. This is replication lag, and it's one of the trickiest problems in distributed databases.
Let me show you what happens when this breaks. The leader just crashed. No more writes. No more replication stream. Your application is stuck.
The leader is down. You have two followers with almost-current data. What do you do?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you pick which follower becomes the new leader?

segments.text: Follower promotion! You pick the follower that's most caught up, promote it to leader, and redirect all writes there. The other follower starts replicating from the new leader. Crisis handled.

So here's your takeaway: replication gives you fault tolerance and read scalability, but it comes with trade-offs — replication lag and the complexity of failover. Next lesson, we'll dig into synchronous versus asynchronous replication and when to use each.
